chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Classical radio of the thirties and the money motive in television
summary: Wilson recalls Toscanini, Barlow and Wallenstein on radio, says only Lawrence Welk survives on TV now, and blames the networks' selling of time.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: And as I say, when Toscanini was at
NBC and every station had a big -- the CBS Symphony under Howard Barlow, and Toscanini at NBC, and Alfred Wallenstein over at Mutual Broadcasting, broadcasting classical music to the masses.
That period -- see, you couldn't have that now.
Why can't we have that now?
You look at TV -- the only music that can survive on TV now is Lawrence Welk.
Right.
There's no other music that can survive. That's the only opening to that big public taste that has worked.
Why?

Except Channel 4 here, Channel 13 in New York, public stations do put it on, and when they do, they have -- what audience there is, they sure get it. Watching TV, the main fare of the TV is pop, commerically, a product that's made to make a buck today and a different product tomorrow to make another buck tomorrow -- that type of thing.
Why do you think that is, Teddy?
We know it's because of the administration, the people who administer, but why do we allow them to do that? The airwaves belong to the people.
Well, for the money. They guys who are making a buck is the whole thing -- they don't mean

any harm, but they're trying to pay their rent, too, just like the virtuosos on the violin, the guys sitting down there overdubbing with gimmicks and looking for a new gimmick to sell tomorrow, a trick, a ...

Well, don't you think it's possible that they can compile stuff sometimes? An example is they took a successful show like the Ed Sullivan Show at its peak and took it off the air because it had been on a long time, and they said well, we just want to do something else.
Well, that was because the money was diminishing. That's the whole thing at CBS -- I was on staff there; you were, too.
Sure.

The only thing they cared about is they is selling that time. And whatever they can get away with legally, they will do anything up there that won't be against the law to sell time, to make that money.
Uh huh. Well, in the advertisement billing, then ...

Well, see, what's been going on up there -- ABC was running away with all the shows and they were hiring and firing the top brass at NBC, and everybody's trying to get up and get those audiences watching these shows to keep the money flowing in. That's the whole motivation of the television and radio world. It's money. Except for the
public channels, you know? Like WQXR.
